title: Revise and leave a reproducible work record
objective: Preserve an initial attempt, document a specific evidence-based revision, and produce a concise final record with inputs, method, result, checks and next action.
why: Future you is a reader of today's work. A reproducible record saves the inputs, reasoning, checks, and reasons for revision, so a corrected answer becomes a reusable lesson instead of an unexplained number.

sections.heading: Quick recall
paragraphs: Preserve the original claim. Name the evidence that prompted review. Explain the exact change, then write the corrected inputs, method, result, units, checks, assumptions, and next action. A short clear record is more useful than a long list of unexplained arithmetic.

Use the practical editor to save a draft, self-check it, and record completion. A fresh task retains the last completed artifact. Showing that task's possible review marks it assisted; completing a fresh task without that review is recorded as independent self-checked work.

sections.heading: Keep a useful before-and-after history
paragraphs: Do not erase a mistake merely to make the page look clean. Quote or summarize the earlier claim, identify its first unsupported step, and say why the new reasoning is better supported. A revision such as 'changed answer to 120' omits the evidence; 'converted 2 h to 120 min because the quotient had hour units' explains the cause.

A calculation correction and a model change are different events. Fixing a unit conversion leaves the supplied model intact. Adding previously excluded timestamps changes the storage boundary. Label which happened, since a new model can legitimately produce a different result without an earlier arithmetic error.

sections.heading: Make the final record reproducible
paragraphs: Include the task or scenario identifier, input meanings and units, equation or procedure, substitution, and final quantity. Then add at least one independent check and a statement of the main limitation. The practical editor saves the scenario seed and completion time with your artifact.

Use clear names and short sentences rather than unexplained abbreviations. If another learner cannot tell whether a rate is per channel, whether time is in minutes, or whether a tank started empty, the record needs one more label. Put extended derivations in lesson notes and keep private personal information out of shared examples.

sections.heading: Choose a concrete next action
paragraphs: A next action resolves a specific uncertainty or practices a specific weakness: measure the rate at two later times, confirm whether metadata is included, or solve a fresh conversion without the worked example. 'Be more careful' does not say what to do.

Decide which result is conditional and what condition matters. If a filling estimate assumes constant inflow, observing the rate during the interval is relevant. Increasing calculator precision will not resolve a changing-rate assumption. Match the next action to the source of uncertainty.

sections.heading: Use completion evidence honestly
paragraphs: The app can verify that required fields and self-check acknowledgments exist. It cannot judge the correctness of every open-ended explanation. Read your artifact against the criteria before checking them; the status is a practical work record, not a numerical mastery score or engineering approval.

Save before navigating away and export progress when you need a portable backup. Ordinary notes, active drafts, and the last completed artifact use the existing progress backup. Revising the active work requires recording completion again; the prior completed artifact remains available until replaced by a newly completed task.

examples.title: Preserve a unit-conversion correction
examples.scenario: An earlier note reports 30/15 = 2 min for a 30 km trip at 15 km/h.

steps.action: Original: '30/15 = 2 min.' Review trigger: in 2 min at 15 km/h, only 0.5 km would be traveled.
steps.reason: The old claim and a scale-based contradiction explain why a revision is necessary.

steps.action: Revision: the quotient is 2 h, so multiply by 60 min/h to obtain 120 min. No input or constant-speed assumption changed.
steps.reason: This identifies the exact conversion error and separates it from a change in the model.

steps.action: Final record: d = 30 km, v = 15 km/h; t = d/v = 2 h = 120 min. Check vt = 30 km. Assumes no stops. Next, confirm whether the requested time includes waiting.
steps.reason: A reader can reproduce both the calculation and the boundary of the result.

examples.conclusion: The revision teaches a reusable lesson: carry the quotient's units through the conversion instead of attaching the requested label afterward.

examples.title: Repair a channel interpretation
examples.scenario: A first draft assumes one channel at 600 samples/s for 10 s at 2 bytes/sample. The task actually specifies three such channels.

steps.action: Original: B = 600 × 10 × 2 = 12,000 bytes. Review trigger: rereading shows the rate applies to each of three channels.
steps.reason: The arithmetic was correct for the assumed one-channel situation, but the input interpretation did not match the task.

steps.action: Correction: include N = 3, so B = 3 × 600 × 10 × 2 = 36,000 bytes.
steps.reason: The revision is traceable to a supplied count, not an unexplained adjustment.

steps.action: Check by adding three identical 12,000-byte payloads. State that headers are excluded; next confirm whether the required storage is payload or complete-file size.
steps.reason: An independent grouping checks the correction while leaving the boundary question visible.

examples.conclusion: Preserve both the original assumption and the task evidence that replaced it. A new number alone cannot communicate that distinction.

examples.title: Revise a changing-rate model
examples.scenario: A tank starts at 10 L and targets 50 L. A draft assumes 5 L/min throughout. Later observations show 5 L/min for the first 4 min, then 4 L/min.

steps.action: Original model: added volume is 40 L, so constant 5 L/min predicts 8 min. New evidence: rate changes after 4 min.
steps.reason: The old calculation follows from its assumption. The observation calls for a model revision, not a claim that 40/5 was wrong.

steps.action: First interval adds 20 L. The remaining 20 L takes 5 min at 4 L/min. Revised total time is 4 + 5 = 9 min.
steps.reason: Splitting the interval respects the supplied piecewise rate instead of averaging rates without considering time.

steps.action: Check final volume: 10 + 5 × 4 + 4 × 5 = 50 L. Next, check whether 4 L/min remains steady during the second interval.
steps.reason: The volume balance verifies the revised result, while the next observation addresses its remaining assumption.

examples.conclusion: A reproducible revision records when the rate changes and which interval each rate describes.

examples.title: A concise handoff paragraph
examples.scenario: Prepare a final record for four channels at 300 samples/s each, recording 25 s at 2 bytes/sample.

steps.action: Write: 'For raw payload only, N = 4, r = 300 samples/(channel·s), T = 25 s, w = 2 bytes/sample. B = NrTw = 60,000 bytes, or 60 decimal kB.'
steps.reason: Input meanings, method, result, and unit convention are present in a compact form.

steps.action: Add: 'A channel contributes 7500 samples or 15,000 bytes; four such contributions agree. Doubling duration would double payload.'
steps.reason: The handoff contains checks a reader can follow without trusting the final multiplication.

steps.action: Close: 'Assumes continuous sampling without compression; metadata is excluded. Next, confirm timestamp format before estimating whole-file size.'
steps.reason: The limitation and next action prevent the payload estimate from being mistaken for a complete capacity requirement.

examples.conclusion: A useful handoff is concise because each sentence has a purpose, not because the evidence has been removed.

guided.prompt: A draft for three channels at 200 samples/s each, 10 s, and 2 bytes/sample says only '4000 bytes; confident.' Turn it into a revision record.
steps: Retain the earlier claim and identify what it counted.
Explain the correction and write a reproducible final calculation.
Add a second check, a limitation, and a next action.
review: Original claim: 4000 bytes. It counted only one channel, so confidence did not supply the missing channel factor.
Revision: B = 3 × 200 × 10 × 2 = 12,000 bytes of raw payload.
Check three equal 4000-byte contributions. Assume continuous sampling; exclude headers. Next confirm whether the requested file size includes per-sample timestamps.

fields.label: Original attempt and what prompted review
fields.help: Keep the original claim and name the check or new fact that prompted review.

fields.label: Specific change and the evidence for it
fields.help: Explain the specific correction or model change and why it is justified.

fields.label: Reproducible final explanation
fields.help: Include input meanings and units, method, calculation, and final result.

fields.label: Independent check and next action
fields.help: Give an independent check, a remaining limitation, and an action that addresses it.

rubric.label: I retained the original claim and explained the revision.
Another learner can reconstruct my inputs, units, method and result.
I recorded an independent check, a model limitation and a concrete next action.

summary: Preserve the original claim and the evidence for a revision.
Distinguish a calculation correction from a model or boundary change.
Save enough inputs, units, method, and checks for another learner to reproduce the work.
Treat recorded completion as self-checked practical evidence; use fresh tasks for independent practice.
retrieval: After a delay, read only one of your old final results. Try to reconstruct its inputs and assumptions, then compare with the saved record and improve any missing explanation.
